passage:
In the last week of November, the cold settled over the small town of Palampur, and Vishal was sitting in the shed office of the tea-packaging startup when the call came from Usha. She had put in the first money two years ago.

"I've decided to step back from the next round," Usha said. "The numbers haven't moved the way we hoped."

Vishal's throat closed. It felt like being left at a bus stop. He stared at the pile of unsold boxes for a long moment.

Then he said, "Thank you for being straight with me. Could you tell me what you saw in the numbers? And is there anyone you'd introduce me to?"

Usha paused. "Ring me next Monday. I'll have two names and some honest feedback."

After the call Vishal wrote a thank-you note on the back of a packing slip, to type up later. He didn't feel better yet, but nothing had been burned.

qa.q: Where was Vishal when Usha called?
qa.a: Vishal was in the shed office of the tea-packaging startup in Palampur.

qa.q: What did Usha's decision feel like to Vishal?
qa.a: It felt like abandonment, like being left at a bus stop, shown by his throat closing and his long stare at the unsold boxes.

qa.q: What did Vishal do that kept the relationship open?
qa.a: Vishal thanked Usha, asked for candid feedback on the numbers and asked for introductions, so the bridge stayed intact.

qa.q: How might Usha see her decision and Vishal's response?
qa.a: Usha probably sees stepping back as a business choice, and Vishal's calm thanks probably makes it easier for her to offer help and honest feedback.

grounding: An investor steps back; Vishal feels abandoned but treats it as a business choice, thanks Usha and asks for feedback and introductions.

"Jagdish, I wanted to tell you in person. I won't be joining the next round."
"Oh." Jagdish set down his cup. "Right."
"It's not personal. My fund is shifting to health tech. Your farm-tools company doesn't fit anymore."
Jagdish felt his throat tighten. Jomon had been the first to believe in him. "You were the first cheque. I... feel a bit left."
"I understand. I'd feel the same."
Jagdish breathed. "Thank you for backing us when no one else would. Can I ask you something?"
"Anything."
"What would you have needed to see to stay? Be blunt."
"Faster sales outside Kerala. And a stronger finance head."
"That's useful. Would you introduce me to anyone who might be a better fit?"
Jomon smiled. "Two people. I'll send the emails today."
"I'd like to stay in touch."
"You'd better."

qa.q: What is Jomon's fund shifting to?
How did Jagdish feel when Jomon said he was stepping back?
qa.a: Jagdish felt hurt and a bit abandoned, his throat tightening, because Jomon had been the first to believe in him.

qa.q: How did Jagdish respond in a way that kept the bridge open?
qa.a: He thanked Jomon, asked for blunt feedback on what would have kept him, and asked for introductions to better-fit investors.

qa.q: How might Jomon see Jagdish's response?
qa.a: Jomon probably respects the grace and maturity, which makes him willing to send introductions and stay in touch.

grounding: An investor steps back; the protagonist feels abandoned but thanks him, asks for candid feedback and introductions, and keeps the bridge intact.

passage:
I'm Vishal, and I remember the exact bench in Cubbon Park where Hemant told me he wouldn't invest in our second round. He'd been our biggest backer. I felt like a kid whose parent had walked out of a school play halfway through.
I wanted to say something bitter. I almost said, "Thanks for nothing." Instead, after a long silence, I said, "Thank you for everything so far. You took a chance on us early." Then I asked him the question I was scared of: "What made you decide?"
He told me straight. Our costs were too high and our pitch was vague. It hurt to hear. It was also true.
He introduced me to an angel investor in Chennai who later came in. Two years on, Hemant invited me to speak at his fund's founder day. I'm glad I didn't burn that bridge on the bench.

qa.q: Where did Hemant tell Vishal he wouldn't invest?
qa.a: On a bench in Cubbon Park.

qa.q: How did Vishal feel when Hemant stepped back?
qa.a: Vishal felt hurt and abandoned, like a kid whose parent walked out of a school play.

qa.q: What did Vishal do that kept the relationship alive?
qa.a: Vishal thanked Hemant, asked for honest feedback, and accepted an introduction instead of saying something bitter.

qa.q: How might Hemant have seen Vishal's reaction on the bench?
qa.a: Hemant probably felt relieved and respectful that Vishal responded with thanks and questions, which made him willing to help later.

grounding: An investor steps back; the protagonist feels abandoned, but thanks him, asks for feedback and introductions, and keeps the bridge open.
